concepts.name: Moral versus non-moral questions
concepts.summary: Distinguish questions of right, wrong and value from questions of fact, taste or law.

concepts.name: Descriptive versus normative claims
concepts.summary: Explain the difference between describing how people behave and claiming how they should behave.

concepts.name: Moral reasons and justification
concepts.summary: Understand that a moral position needs supporting reasons rather than mere assertion or feeling.

concepts.name: Consequentialist idea
concepts.summary: Explain that consequentialism judges actions by the goodness of their outcomes.

concepts.name: Deontological idea
concepts.summary: Explain that deontology judges actions by their conformity to duties, rules or rights.

concepts.name: Virtue ethics idea
concepts.summary: Explain that virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do and focuses on traits.

concepts.name: Moral dilemma
concepts.summary: Recognise a situation where moral considerations conflict and no option satisfies them all.

misconceptions.text: Ethics is just a matter of personal feelings, so no moral view can be better supported than another.
Whatever is legal is morally right, and whatever is illegal is wrong.
Because people disagree about what is right, there is no point reasoning about ethics.

concepts.name: Categorical imperative tests
concepts.summary: Apply Kant's universalisability and treat-people-as-ends tests to a proposed action.

concepts.name: Rights and duties
concepts.summary: Explain how rights and corresponding duties constrain what may be done to people.

concepts.name: Virtues and the mean
concepts.summary: Identify a virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency and apply it to a situation.

concepts.name: Stakeholder identification
concepts.summary: List who is affected by a decision and how, including those without a voice.

concepts.name: Utilitarian calculation
concepts.summary: Apply the utilitarian principle to a simple case by identifying affected parties and comparing total benefits and harms.

concepts.name: Moral relativism versus universalism
concepts.summary: Contrast the view that morality depends on culture with the view that some standards apply to everyone.

concepts.name: Intention versus outcome
concepts.summary: Distinguish what an agent intended from what resulted and show how each framework weighs them.

misconceptions.text: Utilitarianism means doing whatever benefits the majority, regardless of cost to individuals.
Kantian ethics simply means following whatever rules exist, including laws and customs.
The virtuous mean is always moderation or the midpoint between two extremes in a numerical sense.

concepts.name: Act versus rule consequentialism
concepts.summary: Analyse how evaluating individual acts differs from evaluating rules by their general consequences.

concepts.name: Conflicting duties resolution
concepts.summary: Analyse cases where duties clash and explain how to weigh them as prima facie obligations.

concepts.name: Doing versus allowing harm
concepts.summary: Analyse whether causing harm differs morally from allowing it, including intended versus foreseen effects.

concepts.name: Framework comparison on cases
concepts.summary: Analyse a dilemma through consequentialist, deontological and virtue lenses and identify where they agree and diverge.

concepts.name: Trolley problem variants
concepts.summary: Use thought experiments to isolate which morally relevant features drive intuitions.

concepts.name: Moral argument reconstruction
concepts.summary: Break a moral argument into premises, factual and normative, and conclusion to find where it is weak.

concepts.name: Objections to each framework
concepts.summary: Identify the standard objections to each major framework, such as demandingness, rigidity and action-guidance.

misconceptions.text: Rule consequentialism is just deontology under another name.
Killing and letting die are morally identical whenever the outcome is the same.
If a framework produces a counterintuitive verdict in one case, it is refuted.

concepts.name: Reflective equilibrium
concepts.summary: Evaluate and adjust principles and case judgements against each other to reach a coherent position.

concepts.name: Moral uncertainty
concepts.summary: Evaluate how to act when unsure which ethical theory is correct.

concepts.name: Contractualism and social contract
concepts.summary: Analyse justification by principles no one could reasonably reject and the veil of ignorance.

concepts.name: Care ethics and relational views
concepts.summary: Analyse how care ethics emphasises relationships, dependence and context against impartial theories.

concepts.name: Metaethical positions
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing accounts of the status and meaning of moral claims.

concepts.name: Applied ethics case judgement
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing arguments in applied domains and judge which position is best supported.

concepts.name: Justice and fairness theories
concepts.summary: Analyse egalitarian, utilitarian, libertarian and desert-based accounts of fair distribution.

misconceptions.text: Metaethical anti-realism entails that anything goes in first-order ethics.
Reflective equilibrium just means keeping your initial intuitions.
Moral uncertainty means one should suspend judgement and not act.

concepts.name: Constructing original arguments
concepts.summary: Create a defended moral position that anticipates and answers the strongest objections.

concepts.name: Hybrid and pluralist theories
concepts.summary: Design or defend an account combining insights from several frameworks with a principled way to resolve conflicts.

concepts.name: Debunking and evolutionary arguments
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether empirical findings about the origins of moral intuitions undermine their evidential weight.

concepts.name: Population and future ethics
concepts.summary: Evaluate arguments about obligations to future and merely possible people, including the repugnant conclusion.

concepts.name: Moral status and expanding circle
concepts.summary: Evaluate criteria for moral standing and judge their application to animals, ecosystems and artificial systems.

concepts.name: Ethical guidance for institutions
concepts.summary: Create decision procedures or policies that embed ethical reasoning under disagreement and uncertainty.

concepts.name: Evaluating philosophical methodology
concepts.summary: Evaluate the reliability of intuitions, thought experiments and consensus as methods in ethics.

misconceptions.text: A sufficiently refined single theory will eventually resolve all moral conflicts without residual tension.
Showing that moral intuitions evolved automatically proves they are false.
Moral status requires being human, so extending concern further is a category error.
